executive_summary: EUR/JPY trades at 182.16 (close, 5 August 2026), down 1.71% over one month, 1.95% over three months and 1.09% over six months, but still up 2.28% year-on-year and sitting in the 75th percentile of a 164.92–187.96 fifty-two-week range. The defining event is that the cross has just suffered the two most violent sessions of its eighteen-month history: from a 29 July close of 187.42 — 53 sen shy of the April all-time high — it collapsed 8.34 yen (4.45%) to an intraday 179.14 on 3 August as Japan's Ministry of Finance executed an estimated ¥8.45trn yen-buying operation on 30 July and then, on 31 July, the first joint intervention alongside the US since 2011, committing a further $36 billion, with one account stating that Washington participated directly in yen purchases, including selling euros to fund the operation. The bilateral picture that emerges is materially more bearish than either standalone dossier implies: the EUR dossier is tactically bullish EUR at conviction 2 and the JPY dossier is bullish JPY at conviction 4, and the pair inherits the higher-conviction leg. Three differentials do not appear in either dossier — the Bund-JGB 10-year spread has collapsed to just 35bp while the 30-year JGB at 3.971% now yields 31bp more than the 30-year Bund, so the euro's yield advantage exists only inside ten years; the real policy-rate gap is 5bp (−0.65% versus −0.70%) against a 125bp nominal gap, meaning the entire carry is an inflation-differential artefact; and the euro is 8.3% rich to the yen on relative real effective terms, implying a fair value near 167.7–168.8. Most importantly, the intervention has begun re-routing global carry funding out of the yen and into the euro — Morgan Stanley told clients the threat of further yen intervention supports a shift toward the euro and franc as 'funders of choice' — which makes both legs of this specific cross a seller of EUR/JPY rather than the muted signal that two simultaneous speculative shorts would normally imply. We are tactically Bearish at conviction 3 (score −0.2966) targeting 179.00 over two to four weeks, and strategically Bearish at conviction 4 (score −0.3208) targeting 175.00 over six months, with the explicit caveat that Japan's April–May 2026 intervention of ¥11.73trn failed to change trend and that the pair still pays 125bp per annum to be held short.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no direct PPP series for the cross, so we use the relative real-effective method carried in both dossiers: the euro's BIS real broad REER of 102.69 sits 0.5% above its 30-month mean while Japan's at 65.30 sits 7.82% below its own and is the lowest reading ever recorded for the yen on that measure. The euro is therefore 8.3% rich to the yen, implying a relative-REER fair value of 167.7–168.8 versus spot 182.16 — an 8.0–8.6% overvaluation and the largest single valuation gap in the euro's cross matrix and the second largest in the yen's (behind AUD/JPY at 14.2%). Two institutional anchors give the number teeth: Japanese corporates plan to a June Tankan FY2026 assumption of USD/JPY 152.57 and the ten major life insurers to 154, both far stronger than spot, and US Treasury Secretary Bessent said the yen is 'very undervalued' and that excess volatility is not healthy. What is priced at 182 is the assumption that a 125bp nominal carry gap justifies a permanent 8% real-effective dislocation, despite the real policy-rate gap being 5bp.

market_context.recent_regime: Through 29 July the regime was a textbook carry grind: the cross climbed steadily from the 23 June low near 183.15 to 187.42, with daily ranges of 50–90 sen and a roughly 125 basis point gap prompting traders to use the low-yielding yen as a funding currency to finance purchases of higher-yielding currencies like the euro. That regime ended on 30 July with the widest daily range in eighteen months and was extended on 3 August when the yen rose 1% in the Asian morning to 155.20 per dollar, its strongest in about three months, and also advanced against the euro and sterling, stirring speculation Japanese authorities could be in the market again. The dominant narrative for the next month is whether official flow plus a hawkish Bank of Japan can convert a squeeze into a trend, against an ECB that is still hiking and a market that has begun to substitute the euro for the yen as its funding leg.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The annualised carry on a long EUR/JPY position is +125bp (ECB deposit rate 2.25% versus BoJ overnight call target 1.00%), the smallest positive carry available to a long position in any major euro cross except EUR/SEK and a third of the AUD/JPY differential. On money-market rates the gap is roughly 135–142bp. Using a pre-event 3M IV estimate of 8.0, carry-to-vol is +0.16; at the post-intervention realised rate of 10.0% it falls to +0.125. EUR/JPY offers the weakest carry-to-vol of any high-conviction yen cross while charging the cheapest absolute cost to be short — 125bp per annum, less than half USD/JPY's 262.5bp and under 40% of AUD/JPY's 335bp — making it the cheapest carry-adjusted way to own the yen-strength thesis. The carry regime is not dying but rotating: euro-funded carry is thriving (one basket borrowing in euros to buy Brazilian real, Colombian peso and Turkish lira is up roughly 19% in 2026, the most year-to-date since 2005) while yen-funded carry unwinds, which is mechanically bearish EUR/JPY. Forwards already price the pair 1.23 yen lower at six months purely from the rate gap, so a short position starts 123 sen behind spot.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +125bp in the euro's favour (ECB deposit 2.25% versus BoJ target 1.00%) and the level of that gap is unambiguously pair-supportive; the tactical question is the distribution of surprise around it, and that distribution is one-sided. The euro leg is fully priced: the market assigns a 77–83% probability to a 25bp ECB hike on 10 September and a 91.9% cumulative probability of a higher deposit rate by 17 December, so ECB pricing can realistically only fall. The yen leg is barely priced at all: public sources put the 18 September BoJ meeting at somewhere between 16% and 35% and only 21bp of cumulative tightening through December, against a board whose June Summary of Opinions puts neutral 'at around 2 percent' and a Governor who said on 31 July that the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes. Neither meeting falls inside the two-to-four-week window, so the transmission is expectation repricing through four dated releases — the 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, the 20 August Japan national CPI, the 27 August ECB Account and the 1 September euro-area flash HICP — and the asymmetry there favours differential compression. On the curve, the euro's advantage is far narrower than the policy gap implies: the 2-year Schatz at 2.76% versus the 2-year JGB at 1.497% is +126bp, but the 10-year Bund at 3.15% versus the 10-year JGB at 2.801% is only +35bp, and at 30 years the JGB at 3.971% yields 31bp more than the 3.66% Bund. The euro out-yields the yen only inside a decade, which means the pair's rate support is a pure front-end phenomenon that a single BoJ hike materially erodes.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the trajectory is the whole argument, and it points to compression from the yen leg. The ECB is close to the end of its cycle — consensus sees a terminal deposit rate of 2.50–2.75% and the ECB's own June projections have HICP back at 2.0% by 2028 with no second-round effects, a wage tracker at 2.3% and compensation per employee at 3.2% — so the euro has at most 25–50bp to add. Japan sits 100bp below its own board's neutral estimate with a hawkish dissenter already voting for 1.25%, a third consecutive shunto above 5%, and record household and corporate inflation expectations; if the BoJ delivers 50bp by end-Q1 2027 and the ECB 25bp, the differential compresses from 125bp to 100bp, and a 75bp/25bp split takes it to 75bp. On the pair's historical beta to the Bund-JGB 10-year spread, a 25–50bp compression is worth roughly 2.5–5.0 yen. The honest and serious counter-argument is that the rate channel has demonstrably stopped setting the price of the yen: over twelve months the 10-year UST-JGB spread compressed 95bp and the yen still fell 4.92%, and BCA argued that traditional interest-rate differentials no longer explain the yen's weakness, with inflation expectations and the relative steepness of Japan's yield curve providing a stronger explanation for recent moves in USD/JPY and EUR/JPY. That is a direct challenge to this factor's transmission mechanism and is why confidence is 52 rather than 65. The resolution test is observable: if the next leg of the JGB move is led by the 2-year rather than the 30-year, the differential channel is working again and the pair falls with it.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies delivered hawkish data in July, which is why this factor is only mildly bearish for the pair rather than strongly so: the question is not who is accelerating but whose acceleration the market has failed to price. Euro-area July flash HICP printed 2.9% headline, 2.5% core, 3.3% services and 10.0% energy, all accelerating, with Q2 GDP beating at +0.4% q/q and the composite PMI at 51.9 — and the market has already moved ECB September pricing to 77–83% in response. Japan's national core at 1.6% has been below target for five months, but Tokyo July core printed 1.9% against a 1.7% consensus with core-core at 2.0%, and Tokyo leads the national series by roughly a month, so the 20 August national print is likely to show core moving toward 1.8%. The composite PMI comparison actually favours Japan (53.1 versus 51.9), as does the Tankan (large manufacturers +22, best since 2018; non-manufacturers +37, best since 1991). The asymmetric sensitivity is decisive for the pair: because ECB pricing is saturated and BoJ pricing is not, a 20bp upside surprise in Japanese core CPI moves this cross considerably more than a 20bp upside surprise in euro-area HICP. The inflation differential itself — 120bp on headline, 90bp on core, narrowing to roughly 60bp against Tokyo's July core — is the mechanical source of the entire nominal carry, and it is closing.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the composition of the two inflation impulses diverges sharply and it favours the yen. The euro area's overshoot is cost-push and self-liquidating: energy at +10.0% is doing all the work, ex-energy HICP is flat at 2.2%, food is decelerating to 1.2%, the ECB wage tracker is 2.3% for 2026, and Lagarde has said second-round effects are not visible — so the impulse mechanically drops out of the year-on-year comparison during 2027. Japan's impulse is becoming structural: a third consecutive shunto above 5% with 3.50% base pay, nominal earnings above 3% for four consecutive months (longest run since 1992), five months of positive real wages, Tankan corporate price expectations at 2.7%/2.6%/2.6% across one, three and five years, and 90.4% of households expecting higher prices — a series record. The BoJ's own July Outlook cut FY2026 core to 2.5% purely on energy subsidies while raising FY2027 to 2.4% and declaring CPI risks skewed to the upside; BCA expects Japan's headline inflation to reach 2.7% by June 2027, with core inflation rising to 3.1%. If euro-area inflation converges to 2.3% in 2027 while Japan's rises toward 2.4–3.1%, the inflation differential that underwrites the pair's carry inverts. The offset, which is real, is that the euro area grows at roughly three times Japan's year-on-year rate and Japan's potential growth is only 0.5–1.0%, so a BoJ tightening into a fading real-income picture could stall.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/JPY is a moderate-to-high beta risk proxy — the euro is not a haven, the yen is (conditionally), and the cross has historically been among the most equity-correlated of the euro crosses — so the current tape is pair-supportive. The VIX closed at 17.09, US investment-grade spreads are 81bp and high yield 281–287bp, both near cycle tights, the STOXX Europe 600 set a record at 655.45 and the Nikkei 225 at 64,362 is up 23.88% year to date. The critical bilateral observation is that the 4.45% three-session collapse happened with the VIX static and equities at records, which means the pair's risk beta was not the transmission channel — official flow and positioning were. That has two implications: first, the risk factor is currently a support rather than a threat; second, the pair's usual correlation regime is temporarily disrupted, which lowers the information content of this factor. There is also a structural degradation of the classic asymmetry: if the euro is becoming a funding currency alongside the yen, a risk-on impulse now sells both legs and the cross becomes less directional in risk terms than its history implies. The Nikkei channel adds a reflexive twist — Japanese equities have been powered by the weak yen, so yen strength that hits the Nikkei feeds back into risk sentiment and partially offsets the pair-supportive effect of a strong global tape.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months this factor is genuinely two-sided for the cross and forcing a stance would add noise at a 0.05 weight. The bear case for the pair is that volatility distributions sitting in the bottom decile on three separate tenors mean-revert, and EUR/JPY is among the highest-convexity G10 crosses to a carry unwind because it combines a positive-carry long with a haven quote currency. The bull case is that the euro's transition into a funding currency structurally reduces the pair's downside beta to risk-off — if the next shock forces liquidation of euro-funded EM carry, the euro is bought back at the same moment the yen is, and the cross does much less than history suggests. Credit spreads leave no cushion at 81bp and 287bp, but the euro area is not the marginal loser in a global credit event in the way it was in 2011. The Nikkei relationship is the specific channel to watch: a sustained yen rally that breaks the Japanese equity rally would compress Japanese domestic risk appetite and could paradoxically slow repatriation. On balance the classic risk transmission for this pair is being rewired in real time, and Neutral is the honest classification.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the highest-confidence factor in the report and the proximate reason for the tactical stance. Naive netting would say the pair signal is muted because specs are short both legs — leveraged funds short 65,198 EUR contracts and combined yen shorts at 185,047 on the 28 July reports — but the two shorts are not symmetric in their vulnerability or their mechanism. The yen short is beyond its historical extreme threshold of 150,000 contracts, was still growing into the 40-year low, and has now met an unadvertised ¥8.45trn official operation plus, two days later, coordinated action with the US Treasury; the euro short is at a five-year extreme but is a funding position that is being deliberately built, not defended. Both therefore sell EUR/JPY: the yen leg must cover into an official bid, and the euro leg is the new borrowed currency. The single most pair-specific flow in this report is that the US Treasury's participation reportedly involved selling euros to buy yen — an official EUR/JPY sell order from two of the world's largest balance sheets — and Finance Minister Katayama said the action targeted 'excessive volatility and disorderly movements', adding that Japan will not hesitate to conduct further coordinated interventions. The pair's own price action corroborates a forced rather than discretionary unwind: the widest daily range in eighteen months, a break of all three principal moving averages in two sessions, and a nine-month low.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning extremes resolve within weeks, so the strategic question is what the structural bilateral flow balance looks like afterwards, and it is more finely balanced but still tilted lower. Against the pair: the funding rotation into the euro is a multi-quarter allocation decision rather than a trade, Japanese life insurers have told the market that none of the ten majors will add unhedged foreign bonds and that they plan to a 154 USD/JPY assumption, and Japanese corporates have issued a record volume of euro-denominated debt — issuers from Japan sold €18.5 billion of euro-denominated debt in the year to April, more than five times the same period of 2025 — which generates persistent EUR-sell/JPY-buy demand in the basis market as proceeds are swapped home. For the pair: GPIF's announced seven-percentage-point rotation out of JGBs into foreign equities is roughly $52bn of structural yen selling, and Japanese investors have been steady buyers of European debt, having pumped 2.74 trillion yen into European debt securities in the year to November 2025. Reserve-manager demand is a wash-to-negative for both: the yen's share of allocated reserves fell to 5.56% in Q1 2026 and the euro's to 20.03%, so neither currency is winning the diversification flow. Net: the euro's new funding role and Japanese corporate euro issuance outweigh GPIF, but not by enough to justify high confidence.

strategic.contrarian_case: The genuine risk to our strategic view is that the euro's funding-currency role is durable — the ECB ends at 2.50% and stays there while the BoJ stalls again at 1.25% — in which case the euro short persists without ever squeezing and EUR/JPY simply grinds sideways in the 180–186 band. factors.weight_adjustment_reason: −0.02 / −0.03: both economies are large net energy importers, so the commodity channel substantially self-cancels (net +0.3% to +0.6% pair impact per uniform +10% energy move), and bilateral goods trade of $124bn two-way with a $3.6bn net balance is immaterial to either.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor where the standalone dossiers both point the same way against their own currency, and the netting is therefore the whole analysis. Both economies are large net energy importers being taxed by the same shock, so the framework's direction rules must be applied bilaterally rather than in isolation. Net commodity exposure calculation: oil ↑ → −−JPY and −EUR (mild) → net bullish EUR/JPY; LNG/JKM ↑ → −−JPY → net bullish EUR/JPY; TTF gas ↑ → −EUR → net bearish EUR/JPY; coal ↑ → −JPY. Aggregating with Brent at $90.24–91.82 (+26% m/m), TTF at €58.62/MWh (+36% m/m, +66% y/y), JKM at $21.33/MMBtu and Newcastle coal at $134.05/t, a uniform +10% move across the energy complex nets to roughly +0.3% to +0.6% on EUR/JPY, because Japan's exposure is broader (it imports approximately 99% of its oil plus LNG plus coal) while the euro area's is concentrated in gas. The realised evidence supports the sign: Japan's June mineral fuel imports rose 41.9% y/y with petroleum values +59.3% while crude volumes fell 13.7%, and Japan's terms of trade fell 5.0% in a single month to 83.95, 44% below its since-1960 average. Against that, the euro area's monthly goods balance swung €22.8bn year-on-year into a €7.8bn deficit, so the euro is being taxed too, just less severely. Bilateral trade itself is immaterial: IMF DOTS shows EUR exports to Japan of $63.7bn and imports of $60.1bn for 2024, a net euro-area goods surplus of just $3.6bn, so roughly $124bn of two-way trade — under 2% of euro-area external trade and immaterial as a flow driver.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the two forces are large, opposed and roughly equal, which makes this a genuine Neutral rather than a placeholder — and it is the clearest example in this report of two bearish standalone dossier views cancelling at the pair level. Against the pair (yen-supportive): Japan runs a 5.79%-of-GDP current account surplus versus the euro area's 1.7% and falling, holds a record ¥561.75trn net international investment position, and its real effective exchange rate is at an all-time low. For the pair (euro-supportive): Japan's terms of trade are 44% below their historical average with Hormuz LNG transit constrained through end-2026 on Kpler's base case, while the euro area's specific winter risk — storage at 49–55% and roughly ten percentage points behind, the balance-of-summer TTF contract trading €2.68/MWh over Winter 26/27, and the full EU ban on Russian LNG imports landing at end-December — is a euro-negative concentrated in exactly the same quarter. Those two winter squeezes largely offset, and the offsetting is why we cut the strategic weight. The tie-breaker, and the reason we do not lean bullish, is that Japan's surplus is 3.4 times the euro area's and its currency is 8.3% cheaper in real effective terms, so if energy normalises at all the yen has far more room to recover than the euro does.

strategic.what_is_priced: Consensus counts the euro area's energy tax and Japan's record surplus separately and never nets them. factors.horizon_split: The stance flips from mildly Bullish to Neutral because the tactical horizon is dominated by the flow of an active energy price shock that hits Japan harder, while the strategic horizon is dominated by the stock of a 409bp current-account differential and an 8.3% real-effective valuation gap that both favour the yen. The two roughly cancel over six months, which is exactly why we reduced the strategic weight from 0.16 to 0.13.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Strategic +0.02: the widest bilateral divergence in the report — an ECB whose hawkishness is fully capitalised versus a BoJ priced at 21bp cumulative against a ~2% stated neutral, plus a two-treasury official reaction function that has no euro equivalent.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Guidance divergence is the cleanest bilateral asymmetry in this report because it is not about who is more hawkish — both are — but about which hawkishness the market has paid for. The ECB's 23 July statement asserts that inflation risks are to the upside, Lagarde disclosed that some governors questioned whether a hike should be considered, and Schnabel has said rates are not yet restrictive; the market has responded by pricing September at 77–83%, so the ECB's credibility is already fully capitalised and can only disappoint. The BoJ held 8-1 on 31 July with Takata dissenting for 1.25%, Ueda said the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes if conditions are accommodative and that it would debate policy from the next meeting onward, and the July Outlook declared CPI risks skewed to the upside — and the market prices September at 16–35%. There is also a third guidance channel that exists only for the quote currency: an official reaction function backed by two treasuries. One strategist judged that the yen's momentum will last as long as September or October if the Bank of Japan raises rates, adding that the intervention looks paired with BoJ hikes, and Katayama has explicitly refused to name a trigger level while promising further coordinated action. Sequencing cuts the other way inside the window: the ECB meets on 10 September, eight days before the BoJ, so the euro leg gets to set the tone first — but that also means the ECB's hike is a sell-the-fact event immediately before the BoJ's larger surprise potential.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market applies a heavy historical credibility discount to the BoJ and none to the ECB. That relative discount is the pair's mispricing: on 10 August the Summary of Opinions can narrow it without any policy action, and there is no equivalent instrument on the euro side.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.14 strategic weight this becomes the second-largest contributor and the argument is about institutional trajectory rather than rhetoric. The ECB has published an explicit reaction function, anchored expectations at 2%, and hiked unanimously into a shock — high credibility, but credibility that terminates at 2.50–2.75% because its own projections return HICP to 2.0% by 2028. The BoJ has 100bp of latent tightening against its own stated neutral, a published QT path that halts tapering at ¥2trn per month from April 2027, and a Governor who frames delay as the greater risk. Added to that is a reaction function the euro simply does not have: two 2026 interventions totalling roughly ¥20trn, the US Treasury endorsing normalisation and describing substantial yen undervaluation, and now coordinated action. The sceptical case is well evidenced and caps confidence at 55: the roughly $150 billion spent since 2022 shows Japan's commitment is real but has not produced a lasting trend reversal, the Takaichi government's 352-seat supermajority was won on an expansionary platform, and the Cabinet Office asked the BoJ to act while understanding the government's initiatives. Even so, adding US coordination into the mix raises the cost of speculative re-engagement, which is a durable change in the option-adjusted cost of being long this cross.

strategic.what_is_priced: Consensus prices an ECB that stops at 2.50–2.75% correctly and a BoJ that stops at 1.25% incorrectly, and prices intervention as a level defence rather than as a change in the reaction function. Our divergence is that the official bid plus a hawkish board is a two-sided commitment device that raises the required carry to justify a long EUR/JPY position well above 125bp.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bearish, with confidence easing from 58 to 55 because the tactical case rests on three dated BoJ publications inside four weeks that can narrow the pricing gap without any policy action, whereas the strategic case requires the BoJ actually to deliver against an expansionary government — the exact thing it has under-delivered on for three years. The weight doubles from 0.07 to 0.14, so the strategic contribution is larger despite the lower confidence.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The event set inside four weeks is dense but genuinely two-sided for this cross. Pair-negative: the 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, the 20 August Japan CPI, the late-August MoF intervention disclosure that will confirm or refute the ¥8.45trn estimate, and the standing risk of a repeat coordinated operation which Katayama has promised not to hesitate over. Pair-positive: the 14 August euro-area Q2 GDP t+45 estimate, the 27 August ECB Account, the 1 September euro-area flash HICP, and above all any renewed Middle East escalation, since the US-Iran conflict transmits to Japan's import bill more directly than to the euro area's. There is essentially no bilateral political risk between the two economies — no trade dispute, no sanctions, no diplomatic friction — which is unusual and means the pair's event risk is entirely imported from third parties. Event clustering is the specific hazard: the ECB on 10 September and the BoJ on 18 September sit eight days apart, so an ECB hike followed by a BoJ hike would first widen the differential to 150bp and then return it to 125bp, producing a whipsaw of two to three yen in each direction. Asymmetric exposure favours the yen having the larger event set: Japan carries the intervention put and the positioning extreme, while the euro's largest binary (the French budget) is not dated until the autumn.

tactical.what_is_priced: Because the pair's implied volatility was 7–8 into a week containing an FOMC, a BoJ meeting and an active shooting war, the market priced almost no event premium and has only partially repriced since. The tail set is more numerous on the bearish side but larger in magnitude on the bullish side, which is why we hold Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the dated calendar densifies on both legs and the net remains close to balanced. Pair-negative: three BoJ meetings (18 September, 30 October with an Outlook Report, 18 December), the September Tankan on 1 October, and the French PLF 2027 sequence culminating in the 17 November solemn vote, which we treat as a 20–25% probability censure-and-dissolution binary that would take OAT-Bund from 82bp through 130bp and historically drags the euro 1.0–1.5% lower against everything. Pair-positive: the ECB's 10 September and 17 December projection rounds, the end-December EU ban on Russian LNG imports arriving with euro-area storage roughly ten points behind, and continued Hormuz constraint — though the last of these is ambiguous, since restricted LNG hurts Japan as directly as Europe. The euro area's autumn is politically busier than Japan's: German state elections on 20 September, French Senate elections on 27 September, four French rating reviews between 28 August and 27 November, and the 17–18 December European Council. Japan by contrast has no scheduled national election inside the window. That means the euro carries more dated political risk and Japan carries more policy risk, and the two roughly offset at a 0.05 weight.

Confidence eases from 52 to 50 because the six-month window admits a wider set of unknowable escalations without changing the two-sidedness.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both sovereigns are stressed, and for this pair the crucial point is that fiscal stress has been currency-negative for the yen and only latently currency-negative for the euro. Japan's 30-year JGB at 3.971% sits within 4bp of its all-time high, the FY2026 budget is a record ¥122.3trn with debt-service costs assumed at a 29-year-high 3.0% rate, and the government has revised consolidated debt to 187.6% of GDP — and the acceleration in 30-year and 40-year Japanese government bond yields suggests markets are repricing sovereign risk and inflation persistence simultaneously. That is the mechanism by which higher Japanese yields have coincided with a weaker yen, and it is pair-supportive. On the euro side, France's OAT at 3.98% is at a 17-year high with OAT-Bund at 82bp now trading through Italy, but no French fiscal event is dated before the 30 September Conseil des ministres, and the only item inside the window is Fitch's 28 August review. The rating differential is worth noting precisely because it is narrower than it looks: Germany is AAA but the marginal sovereign for the euro is France at A+/Aa3-negative, only one to two notches above Japan's A1/A+/A — and Japan's ratings are all stable while two French agencies carry negative outlooks. Tactically, the live premium is Japanese and the dormant premium is European, so the factor tilts pair-positive.

Inside four weeks the Japanese premium is live and the French one is not, which is mildly pair-supportive.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the two fiscal risks become comparable in size and opposite in sign for the pair, which resolves to a genuine Neutral. The euro's binary is dated and quantifiable: the PLF 2027 solemn vote on 17 November with a 20–25% censure-and-dissolution path that would take OAT-Bund through 130bp weeks before a presidential campaign, plus four French rating reviews and a German 2027 budget carrying €109.7bn of defence spending. Japan's risk is continuous rather than binary: refinancing a 187.6%-of-GDP debt stock at 30-year yields near 4% while the BoJ shrinks its holdings from ¥518trn to a projected ¥480trn by March 2027, with a board member publicly warning that halting the taper risks purchases being perceived as fiscal financing. The bilateral netting depends on which channel dominates: a French crisis is euro-negative and pair-negative; a Japanese long-end break above 4.25% is yen-negative and pair-positive. Both are roughly 20% probability events with roughly comparable currency impact, and each has a partial mitigant — Japan's ~90% domestic ownership and stable ratings, the euro area's Transmission Protection Instrument and Spain's re-rating. Neutral is the honest classification and it is argued rather than defaulted.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Tactical +0.02: the pair has just broken beneath a converged 50/100/200-day cluster with a confirmed lower high, and sits 1.76 yen above the 55-week EMA that defines its medium-term trend classification.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The pair's own chart has just delivered the most significant structural break of the eighteen-month sample, and unusually for a technical factor it is corroborated by price data rather than inferred. Spot at 182.16 is below the 50-day (184.785), 100-day (184.909) and 200-day (184.574) simultaneously, and those three averages sit within a 34-sen band — a converged, trendless configuration that has been resolved lower, which removes systematic trend support and arms a bearish crossover. The higher-high sequence has failed: the 29 July peak of 187.475 came 48 sen below the 17 April all-time high of 187.9575, and the 3 August low of 179.14 is the weakest since mid-November 2025, giving the first lower-high-plus-lower-low structure since June 2025. Web-sourced chart analysis marks the decisive medium-term level at the 55-week EMA of 180.40, whose break would reclassify the trend, and the broken range floor at 183.20–183.50 as the first resistance. Volatility corroborates: realised has tripled from roughly 4% to roughly 10% while the 30 July session produced the widest daily range in the sample; the variance risk premium is now negative, meaning spot rather than options is the efficient expression. The risk-reversal skew already favours EUR/JPY puts (yen calls) as the standing intervention hedge, so the downside wing is not cheap — a materially different configuration from USD/JPY, where the JPY dossier finds implied volatility badly lagging realised.

The exploitable observation is that a converged MA cluster resolved lower with a confirmed lower high is a high-probability continuation structure, and the 183.20–183.50 shelf gives an unusually tight and unambiguous invalidation level 1.0–1.3 yen above spot.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the structure is a trend-classification question with a single identified test level. The uptrend from the 2020 low remains formally intact and the bull-case extension is well specified — the bigger-picture uptrend from 114.42 is still expected to resume at a later stage toward a 78.6% projection at 194.88 — but the reclassification trigger is close and specific: a sustained break of the 55-week EMA at 180.40 would argue the cross is already in a medium-term downtrend targeting 175.41 and below. Spot is 1.76 yen above that line, and the 3 August low of 179.14 has already traded through it intraday without closing beneath it on a weekly basis. The MA configuration reinforces the asymmetry: because the 50-, 100- and 200-day averages are converged rather than stacked, a sustained two-to-three-yen decline flips all three into a bearish stack within weeks, whereas a recovery must clear 2.6 yen of overhead average before the trend reasserts. Volatility term structure is backwardated into the August–September event cluster and prices no premium for the November–December cluster (French budget, twin central bank projection rounds, Russian LNG ban), so longer-dated optionality is cheap relative to its risk content even though short-dated is not.

expression_assessment.vol_landscape_summary: Negative variance risk premium for this cross: realised (~10%) running above a pre-event implied strip of 7–9 that has since repriced higher; risk reversals favour EUR/JPY puts (yen calls) as the standing intervention hedge, making the downside wing the expensive side; term structure is backwardated near-term into the August–September event cluster but flat with no premium priced for the November–December cluster.
expression_assessment.directional_expression: Express the tactical view in spot or forwards rather than options — the opposite prescription to the USD/JPY leg. Buying convexity now means paying for a move that has already begun, and the skew is against the buyer of the view. The invalidation level is unusually tight and unambiguous at 183.20–183.50 (one yen above spot) with the MA cluster at 184.57–184.91 immediately behind, allowing a spot short to be risk-managed for 1.0–2.6 yen against a 3.2-yen base-case objective. For the strategic horizon the calculus flips: three-to-six-month optionality is cheap relative to its risk content given the flat term structure into November–December, and is the more efficient way to hold the six-month view because it caps gap risk the short-carry forward position cannot.
expression_assessment.event_timing_consideration: Any structure should expire after 18 September, and dating it beyond 10 September avoids being stopped by the ECB-first sequencing. Gap risk is material: coordinated official intervention produces 3–5 yen sessions with no intervening liquidity, and both of the two widest daily ranges in eighteen months were intervention days, so a spot position should be sized for a 5-yen adverse gap rather than a 1-yen stop.
expression_assessment.liquidity_note: EUR/JPY is a highly liquid G10 cross, but liquidity can evaporate intraday during coordinated intervention sessions (30 July and 3 August both produced the widest daily ranges of the 390-session sample), so execution should assume episodic gap risk around dated BoJ and MoF events rather than continuous two-way liquidity.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: −0.03 / −0.03: non-USD cross in which both legs are funding currencies with symmetric, benign dollar conditions, and the framework's benchmark cross-currency basis is unobtainable.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: For a non-USD cross the dollar matters through the vehicle-currency channel, and conditions are benign and largely symmetric: SOFR at 3.65% with effective fed funds at 3.63%, an expanding Fed balance sheet at $6,738bn versus $6,614bn in February, IG credit at 81bp, and no drawing on the Fed's standing swap lines with either the ECB or the BoJ. Ample, cheap dollars are the oxygen of carry, and carry in this pair means long EUR/JPY, so benign funding is prima facie pair-supportive. The bilateral complication in this episode is that the dollar's decline was caused by yen buying rather than by dollar weakness — the dollar index fell to a seven-week low of 99.42 on 3 August following the intervention, down 1.0% over the week — and if the operation was partly funded by selling euros, then the same flow that weakened the dollar also weakened the euro against the yen. Normally a falling dollar in a liquid regime lifts EUR/USD (the euro being 57.6% of the DXY) more than it lifts JPY/USD, which raises the cross; this time the causality ran the other way. Netting the two effects gives no clear tactical signal. There is also a genuine data gap: the 3M EUR/USD and JPY/USD cross-currency bases were unobtainable in both dossiers, so the EUR/JPY basis cannot be derived, and the framework's designated benchmark for this factor is missing.

We do not round to 4 because the pair still pays 125bp per annum to be held short; Japan's April–May 2026 intervention of ¥11.73trn was followed by a new 40-year yen low ten weeks later; and the ECB meets eight days before the BoJ, so the sequencing inside September is briefly pair-supportive.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the score is dominated by Policy & Rates at 0.24 and Inflation & Growth at 0.18, which together carry 42% and both point lower for the pair — not because the euro's carry advantage is disappearing but because its pricing is saturated while the yen's is not: a 77–83% priced ECB September hike against a 16–35% priced BoJ hike is an asymmetry in which only one leg can surprise. The +125bp nominal differential that supposedly anchors this cross survives almost entirely in the front end; the 10-year Bund-JGB spread is just 35bp and at 30 years the JGB yields 31bp more than the Bund, while the real policy-rate gap is 5bp (−0.65% versus −0.70%). The two dossiers conflict head-on tactically — both are bullish their own currency — and the pair inherits the higher-conviction leg, but the bilateral case does not rest on that arithmetic: it rests on three things neither dossier contains. First, the coordinated intervention has a direct EUR/JPY transmission, since Washington's participation reportedly involved selling euros to buy yen and Katayama has promised not to hesitate to repeat it. Second, the intervention is re-routing carry funding out of the yen and into the euro, so the pair now has a seller on both legs — normally two simultaneous speculative shorts mute a pair signal, and here they amplify it. Third, the pair's own chart has broken a converged 50/100/200-day cluster with a confirmed lower high at 187.475 (below the April record) and a lower low at 179.14, the first such sequence of the 14-month uptrend. Against this, the pair-supportive factors are real and correctly identified rather than dismissed: the risk tape is benign with equities at records and credit near tights, energy prices tax Japan more than the euro area (net +0.3% to +0.6% per uniform +10% energy move), and Japan's own fiscal risk premium at the long end is currently yen-negative. What is priced is a bounce back into the 183.50–186.00 range that contained July; what we expect is that the 183.20–183.50 broken floor caps the retracement and the pair works toward 179.00, with the edge being that the market is still treating this as a level defence rather than as a change in the official reaction function. The path of least resistance is lower because the marginal buyer of the cross was a yen-funded carry account that has just been liquidated and now faces a higher option-adjusted cost of re-engagement. Dated catalysts are dense and front-loaded: 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, 20 August Japan national CPI, 27 August ECB Account, late-August MoF disclosure, 1 September euro-area flash HICP. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the carry runs against the position, because two prior 2026 interventions failed to change trend, and because spot has already retraced 37% of the drop; it is 3 rather than 2 because the positioning extreme, the official flow and the technical break are observable facts rather than forecasts.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among yen crosses, short EUR/JPY ranks 3rd of eight in the opportunity set. What EUR/JPY uniquely offers is the cheapest carry cost of any major yen-cross short at 125bp — less than half USD/JPY and 37% of AUD/JPY — plus a catalyst none of the others has, namely reported official euro selling and the euro's substitution as the market's funding currency. strategic.score_interpretation: −0.3208 sits in the lower half of the conviction-4 band (0.30–0.45). The structure of the score is unusual and worth stating plainly: five factors contribute exactly zero and none contributes positively. That is not a monotone ballot but the arithmetic of a pair whose offsets cancel internally — External Balance is Neutral at a 0.13 weight because Japan's 5.79% current-account surplus offsets its deeper terms-of-trade damage; Fiscal is Neutral because a dated French binary offsets a continuous Japanese long-end premium; Risk Appetite is Neutral because both currencies are now funding legs; USD Liquidity is Neutral because the basis is unmeasurable. The directional signal therefore comes entirely from the policy and guidance block (Factors 1 and 6, contributing −0.2122 of the −0.3208 on 0.40 of combined weight), reinforced by inflation convergence and the funding rotation. Conviction 4 is justified by the fact that the two largest weights point the same way with the 8.3% valuation gap behind them; overall confidence of 60% rather than higher reflects that Factors 1 and 6 are two expressions of one claim — that the BoJ closes its gap to neutral — and that claim has been wrong for three years.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the dossier is dominated by Policy & Rates at 0.26, External Balance at 0.13 and Guidance at 0.14, and the decisive analytical judgement is that the second of those three cancels itself while the first and third align. The rate case is the trajectory, not the level: the ECB has 25–50bp left to a 2.50–2.75% terminal because its own projections return HICP to 2.0% by 2028 with a 2.3% wage tracker and no second-round effects, while the BoJ sits 100bp below its board's stated ~2% neutral with a third consecutive 5%-plus shunto, record inflation expectations and a dissenter already voting for 1.25% — so a plausible 50bp/25bp split compresses the differential from 125bp to 100bp and a 75bp/25bp split to 75bp, worth 2.5–5.0 yen on the pair's historical spread beta. Guidance reinforces it at nearly double the tactical weight because the credibility discount is asymmetric: the market pays full price for ECB hawkishness and almost nothing for BoJ hawkishness, and the quote currency now additionally enjoys a two-treasury reaction function following the first coordinated intervention in fifteen years. The two dossiers interact constructively here rather than conflicting: the euro's own strategic stance is Neutral (+0.0820) precisely because its energy import bill and French fiscal calendar cap its upside, while the yen's is Bullish (+0.1848) — so unlike the tactical horizon there is no head-on collision, and the pair simply inherits the difference. The bilateral factors that modify both standalone views are the collapsed Bund-JGB curve relationship (35bp at ten years, inverted by 31bp at thirty), the 8.3% relative-REER overvaluation with a fair value of 167.7–168.8, and the euro's structural transition into the market's funding currency of choice, which adds a persistent supply of euros that no published EUR/JPY forecast incorporates. What is priced is a consensus path of roughly 182–183 at end-2026 — essentially flat — built on the assumption that 125bp of carry is a permanent anchor; what we expect is 175.00 at six months, roughly 593 pips below the computed 6M forward of 180.93. The path of least resistance is a descending staircase with a decision point around the 18 September BoJ meeting and a second around the 17 November French vote. Key dated catalysts: 18 September and 30 October BoJ meetings, 10 September and 17 December ECB projection rounds, 1 October September Tankan, 17 November PLF 2027 solemn vote, end-December Russian LNG ban. Conviction is 4 because the two heaviest factors align behind a large and measurable valuation gap with an identified closing mechanism; it is not 5 because the entire case reduces to a single claim about BoJ delivery that the market has repeatedly and rationally discounted, and because BCA's argument that rate differentials no longer explain the yen is a direct, credible challenge to the transmission mechanism.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, short EUR/JPY ranks 2nd of eight in the yen-cross opportunity set, improving from 3rd tactically. It moves ahead of short NZD/JPY because the RBNZ is the one central bank likely to out-hike the BoJ, which erodes that cross's convergence case, and it remains behind short AUD/JPY, where a 14.2% relative-REER gap and 335bp of carry make the valuation payoff larger even though the financing cost is 2.7 times higher. Its relative advantage grows with horizon precisely because carry cost compounds: over six months a short EUR/JPY pays 1.14 yen against 2.4 yen for a short USD/JPY and 3.1 yen for a short AUD/JPY, so on a carry-adjusted basis EUR/JPY is the most efficient way to hold a six-month yen-strength view of any liquid cross. Relative to the euro's own strategic Neutral stance, this is the single cross where the euro's structural weaknesses meet a counterparty at a record real-effective discount.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are aligned in direction and divergent in conviction. The tactical score is diluted by three pair-supportive contributions (Risk Appetite +0.0520, External Balance +0.0208, Fiscal +0.0200) that all turn to Neutral at the strategic horizon once the offsets are properly netted, while the strategic score concentrates weight in the two factors where the bilateral case is strongest (Policy & Rates at 0.26 and Guidance at 0.14, together contributing −0.2122). Mechanically the divergence is created by weight migration plus stance resolution: External Balance moves from mildly Bullish at 0.04 to Neutral at 0.13, Guidance's weight doubles, and Inflation & Growth's halves. Substantively the tactical path is noisier than the strategic direction — post-intervention retracements of 30–50% are normal, the pair has already retraced 37%, the ECB meets eight days before the BoJ, and the energy complex still taxes Japan more than the euro area — all reasons to expect chop inside four weeks. Over six months those noise sources either resolve or cancel, and what remains is a 125bp differential with only front-end support, an 8.3% real-effective overvaluation with an identified closing mechanism, and a funding rotation that supplies euros structurally.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 18 September BoJ meeting, with the 30 October Outlook Report as the confirming event and the 55-week EMA at 180.40 as the price-level equivalent. cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Because both horizons agree on direction, the position can be held rather than time-boxed — but it should be built rather than established at once. Size the tactical leg for the two-to-four-week window with invalidation at 183.50 and gap tolerance for a 5-yen adverse session; add on any failure below 184.00 rather than chasing weakness below 180. Because the two horizons agree, the negative carry of 125bp is tolerable in a way it would not be if only the tactical view were bearish, and it remains the cheapest yen-cross short in the complex. Express the tactical leg in spot/forward (negative variance risk premium, expensive downside wing) and the strategic leg in three-to-six-month optionality, where the surface charges nothing for the November–December cluster and where gap risk from further coordinated operations is capped.

This is the euro's best-dated pair-supportive catalyst inside the window, and its limitation is that 83% is already close to the ceiling.

catalysts.event: MoF monthly FX intervention disclosure (30 July–27 August window)
catalysts.rationale: This confirms or refutes the ¥8.45trn estimate for 30 July and discloses the Japanese side of the coordinated 31 July operation. Tokyo has spent approximately $150 billion in cumulative yen-support operations since 2022, including a $35 billion single intervention in 2024, and the July 2026 tranche of $53 billion surpassed even that; a confirmed figure above ¥10trn would establish the largest operation on record and materially raise the perceived cost of re-establishing a long EUR/JPY carry position.

The decisive input for the 10 September ECB decision. July printed 2.9% headline and 2.5% core with all four components accelerating; a print at or above 2.9% locks the September hike and keeps the differential widening into the BoJ meeting, while a print at or below 2.6% cuts ECB odds below 55% and would compound the pair's decline by removing its only remaining support.

A 25bp hike to 2.50% is 77–83% priced and would widen the differential to 150bp for exactly eight days before the BoJ meets. Because the hike itself is saturated, the pair's reaction depends on the projections: a 2027 HICP revision at or above 2.3% extends the ECB path and is pair-positive, while a revision toward 2.1% caps the cycle and is pair-negative. Classic sell-the-fact risk on the rate with genuine two-sided risk on the forecasts.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: The single largest dated event for this pair and the meeting Ueda pointed at when he said the Bank would debate policy from the next meeting onward. Priced at 16–35% against a fair value the JPY dossier assesses at 45–50%; a hike to 1.25% returns the differential to 125bp eight days after the ECB widened it to 150bp and, more importantly, unlocks pricing for the next step toward a ~2% neutral. One strategist judged the yen's momentum will last as long as September or October if the Bank of Japan raises rates.

The June survey showed large manufacturers at +22 (best since 2018) and non-manufacturers at +37 (best since 1991), with corporate inflation expectations rising at all three horizons. The critical number for this pair is the FY2026 USD/JPY planning assumption of 152.57 — if firms revise it weaker, pass-through to consumer prices accelerates and the BoJ's hand is forced; if they hold it, corporate hedging behaviour becomes a standing yen bid.

catalysts.event: French Assemblée nationale solemn vote on PLF 2027
catalysts.rationale: The largest euro-specific binary in the strategic window and unambiguously pair-negative. A 49.3 invocation without a negotiated majority invites censure; a successful censure means dissolution weeks before a presidential campaign, taking OAT-Bund from 82bp toward 130bp. Historically an OAT-Bund move through 100bp drags the euro 1.0–1.5% lower against all crosses independent of the ECB, and the yen is the natural recipient given its record real-effective discount.

catalysts.event: ECB decision plus Eurosystem projections; BoJ decision; European Council
catalysts.rationale: The densest cluster of the horizon: the ECB (91.9% cumulative probability of a higher deposit rate by this date) and the BoJ (81–84% cumulative probability of one hike) decide within 24 hours of each other, alongside a European Council on the 2028-34 multiannual financial framework. Both legs can move 2–3 yen and the sequencing is unknowable, which is why the honest expression is long volatility rather than a directional position.

catalysts.event: Full EU ban on Russian LNG imports
catalysts.rationale: A self-imposed European supply cut landing with EU storage roughly ten points behind and Hormuz LNG transit constrained. The first-order effect is euro-negative (higher TTF, wider euro-area goods deficit) and therefore pair-negative; the second-order effect is that European competition for Atlantic cargoes lifts JKM, which is yen-negative and pair-positive. Because Europe is the party imposing the cut, we tilt the net to pair-negative.

invalidators.condition: EUR/JPY posts two consecutive daily closes above 183.50 (the broken July range floor)
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's entire technical case rests on the converged 50/100/200-day cluster at 184.57–184.91 having been decisively lost and on 183.20–183.50 flipping from support to resistance; a reclaim frames the 30 July–3 August move as an official-flow spike within an intact range rather than a structural break, and hands the initiative back to the 125bp carry.

invalidators.condition: The 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions reads balanced-to-dovish AND September hike pricing falls below 15% on both public representations while ECB September pricing holds above 80%
invalidators.mechanism: The implied differential would widen toward 150bp with no offsetting yen catalyst before 30 October, and Factors 1 and 6 — 0.31 of tactical weight and 0.40 of strategic weight — would flip sign simultaneously.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: BoJ Summary of Opinions and TONA futures/OIS-implied September probability

invalidators.condition: The MoF disclosure at end-August confirms the 30 July operation below ¥5trn AND no further coordinated action occurs while USD/JPY reclaims 160
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's dominant bilateral catalyst is a change in the official reaction function, not a one-off level defence; a small, unrepeated operation reduces this to the April–May template, after which the yen made a new 40-year low within ten weeks and EUR/JPY rallied 4.5 yen.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF monthly intervention disclosure and USD/JPY versus 160
invalidators.monitor_frequency: monthly for the disclosure, daily for spot

invalidators.condition: Brent sustains above $110 with JKM above $26/MMBtu for ten consecutive sessions while TTF stays below €65/MWh
invalidators.mechanism: That specific combination maximises the asymmetry in the net commodity calculation — Japan's import bill absorbs oil, LNG and coal while the euro area's marginal exposure is gas that is not participating — taking Japan's terms of trade toward the 69.80 record low and widening its goods deficit toward ¥1trn a month.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front-month, JKM spot, TTF front-month

invalidators.condition: The 30-year JGB exceeds 4.25% while EUR/JPY simultaneously trades above 185.00
invalidators.mechanism: This is the definitive confirmation that Japanese yields are a fiscal credit premium rather than a policy premium — the exact configuration that produced 95bp of UST-JGB compression alongside a 4.92% yen decline over the past year — and it voids the rate-convergence mechanism carrying 0.40 of our strategic weight.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF constant-maturity 30-year JGB alongside EUR/JPY spot

invalidators.condition: Euro-area August or September flash HICP prints at or above 3.1% with core at or above 2.6% while Japanese national core falls below 1.4%
invalidators.mechanism: The core inflation differential would widen from 90bp back toward 170bp, re-anchoring the ECB path above 3.00% and removing the convergence thesis that underwrites Factor 2 on both horizons.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Eurostat flash HICP and Japan national CPI

invalidators.condition: EUR/JPY 20-day realised volatility falls back below 5% with spot confined to a 181–184 band for four consecutive weeks
invalidators.mechanism: The carry regime would have been restored intact: at sub-5% realised the pair's carry-to-vol ratio returns above +0.25 and the 125bp differential again dominates a low-volatility grind, which is the environment in which euro-funded long EUR/JPY positions compound.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Realised volatility computed from daily closes; spot range

signposts.confirms_if: compresses below +20bp, or inverts at ten years, led by the Japanese front end
signposts.invalidates_if: widens above +70bp, or compresses only via a rising 30-year JGB while the pair rises
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's own historical primary driver and it matters far more here than for either currency alone, because the euro's yield advantage over Japan now exists only inside a decade — the cross is structurally supported by a front-end gap that a single BoJ hike erodes, a fragility invisible in either dossier's standalone yield tables.

signposts.indicator: Implied Probability of a BoJ Hike on 18 September Relative to ECB Pricing for 10 September
signposts.current_level: BoJ 16–35% (sources conflict); ECB 77–83%; BoJ cumulative tightening to December 21bp
signposts.confirms_if: BoJ September above 50% while ECB September stays at or below 85%
signposts.invalidates_if: BoJ September below 15% while ECB December pricing implies a second hike
signposts.bilateral_importance: The ratio of the two probabilities is the pair's core mispricing and does not appear in either dossier, which each tracks only its own central bank. Because the ECB's number is near its ceiling and the BoJ's is near its floor, all the convexity in the pair's rate factor sits on the quote leg.
signposts.frequency: daily, with step-changes around 10 August, 20 August and 1 September

signposts.indicator: Combined CFTC Positioning: Yen Net Short and Euro Leveraged Net Short
signposts.current_level: JPY combined leveraged + asset manager −185,047 contracts (28 July, OI 432,366); EUR leveraged −65,198 with net specs at $10.3bn short, the most since February 2020
signposts.confirms_if: the yen short falls below 130,000 contracts while the euro short holds or grows — evidence that the funding rotation is real and the pair has a seller on both legs
signposts.invalidates_if: the yen short extends beyond 195,000 contracts, or the euro short is cut below 30,000 while the yen short covers
signposts.bilateral_importance: For this pair the relationship between the two shorts is the signal, not either level. Two simultaneous shorts normally mute a pair signal; here they amplify it, and the confirmation is precisely a divergence in their paths — yen covering alongside euro building.
signposts.frequency: weekly, Friday 15:30 ET for the prior Tuesday

signposts.indicator: EUR/JPY Spot Versus the 55-Week EMA (180.40) and the 50/100/200-Day Cluster (184.57–184.91)
signposts.current_level: spot 182.16, sitting 1.76 yen above the 55-week EMA and 2.41–2.75 yen below the daily MA cluster
signposts.confirms_if: a weekly close below 180.40, which reclassifies the medium-term trend toward 175.41
signposts.invalidates_if: a daily close above 184.91, restoring the pair above all three principal daily averages
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's own chart, not either currency's trade-weighted index, and the configuration is unusually informative because the three daily averages are converged within 0.18% — a 2–3 yen move flips all three into a bearish stack, whereas a recovery must clear 2.6 yen of overhead supply. The band between 180.40 and 184.91 is the entire structural question for the cross.
signposts.frequency: daily, with the weekly close the decisive observation

signposts.indicator: JKM-TTF Spread (Japanese Versus European LNG/Gas Pricing)
signposts.current_level: JKM $21.33/MMBtu (30 July) against TTF at €58.62/MWh (roughly $20.9/MMBtu), with Asian spot LNG reported at a $1.09/MMBtu premium to TTF
signposts.confirms_if: the JKM premium over TTF collapses to zero or inverts — Japan's terms-of-trade disadvantage disappearing removes the pair's main energy support
signposts.invalidates_if: the JKM premium widens beyond $3/MMBtu, meaning Japan is decisively losing the bidding war for flexible cargoes
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the single cleanest bilateral terms-of-trade signpost for EUR/JPY and it exists nowhere in either dossier, which track TTF (euro area) and JKM (Japan) separately. Because both economies are net importers, only the relative price of their marginal energy import moves the cross, and this spread is that price.

signposts.indicator: Ministry of Finance Intervention Disclosures and Evidence of Repeat Coordinated Action
signposts.current_level: estimated ¥8.45trn on 30 July (unconfirmed) plus a reported further $36bn in coordinated action on 31 July; official confirmation of the April–May window was ¥11,734.9bn
signposts.confirms_if: the disclosed 30 July figure exceeds ¥10trn, or a further coordinated operation occurs
signposts.invalidates_if: the disclosure comes in below ¥5trn with no follow-through and USD/JPY reclaims 160
signposts.bilateral_importance: Intervention is a quote-currency event with a direct base-currency transmission for this cross specifically, because the US Treasury's participation reportedly involved selling euros — making EUR/JPY the one major cross where the official operation is executed through the pair rather than merely affecting it.
signposts.frequency: monthly disclosure (end of month for the prior 27th-to-27th window); spot evidence daily

signposts.current_level: 82bp, now trading at or through the 80bp BTP-Bund spread, with the OAT at a 17-year high of 3.98%
signposts.confirms_if: widens through 110bp — historically worth 1.0–1.5% of euro downside independent of the ECB
signposts.invalidates_if: narrows below 70bp, indicating the PLF 2027 process is being absorbed and removing the euro's largest dated binary
signposts.bilateral_importance: French fiscal stress matters more for EUR/JPY than for most euro crosses because the yen is the natural recipient of a European redenomination premium at a record real-effective discount, and because there is no offsetting Japanese political event dated inside the same window.
signposts.frequency: daily; critical around 20 October, 17 November and the 23 October and 27 November rating reviews

signposts.current_level: approximately 10.0% (15-session, computed from the provided daily closes), versus roughly 4% through mid-July
signposts.confirms_if: sustained above 8%, keeping the carry-to-vol ratio below +0.16 and the cross unattractive to funding accounts
signposts.invalidates_if: falls below 5%, restoring carry-to-vol above +0.25 and the low-volatility grind in which long EUR/JPY compounds
signposts.bilateral_importance: For this cross volatility is not a risk metric but the direct determinant of the trade's viability — the entire long-EUR/JPY proposition is 125bp of carry, and at 10% volatility that carry buys a ratio of 0.125, which is not enough to attract the marginal funding account. This is why the volatility regime matters more for EUR/JPY than for either currency's trade-weighted index.
signposts.source: computed from Twelve Data daily OHLC (provided); corroborated by https://cryptobriefing.com/japan-us-currency-intervention-yen-traders/

assumptions: Spot, all performance figures, the 52-week range and percentile, all three moving averages, the trend-regime assessment and all realised-volatility estimates are taken from or computed on the provided Twelve Data daily OHLC series (390 sessions, 12 June 2025 to 5 August 2026). Spot is the 5 August close of 182.16321. The two source dossiers carry a valuation date of 1 August and an EUR/JPY reference of 182.83 at the 31 July close, whereas the price data extends to 5 August at 182.16; all pair-level calculations use 182.16 and all dossier-derived cross-checks are noted as of 31 July. The four-day gap spans the 3 August low of 179.14 and is material to the technical assessment.

Realised volatility is computed as the standard deviation of daily log returns over the final fifteen sessions, annualised at √252, giving approximately 10.0%; the pre-event comparison of approximately 4% is computed the same way on the sessions to 29 July. The series contains some weekend/holiday fills (open=high=low=close), which flattens ranges and biases short-window volatility slightly downward; moving averages are taken as provided.

Implied volatility for EUR/JPY could not be sourced from any citable venue this cycle. The two dossiers carry conflicting estimates for 3M EUR/JPY implied volatility — 9.0 in the EUR dossier and 7.5 in the JPY dossier, both explicitly flagged as estimates — and we therefore quote a pre-event range of 7.0–8.0 for 1M and 7.5–9.0 for 3M and use the midpoint of 8.0 for carry-to-vol. Every carry-to-vol ratio in this report inherits that estimate. The 25-delta risk-reversal sign is inferred from documented USD/JPY skew and the standing intervention hedge; no EUR/JPY magnitude was retrievable and none is asserted.

Forward points are computed, not quoted. No dated market EUR/JPY forward strip was retrievable. We use covered interest parity with a 135bp money-market differential (3M Euribor 2.472% against an assumed 3M yen rate of 1.05–1.10%). The cross-currency basis is excluded because the 3M EUR/USD and JPY/USD bases were unobtainable in both source dossiers, so the EUR/JPY basis cannot be derived — a flagged gap that also caps Factor 10 confidence at 48 on both horizons.

Valuation uses the relative real-effective method carried in both dossiers rather than absolute PPP: the euro's BIS real broad REER deviation from its 30-month mean (+0.49%) less the yen's (−7.82%) gives an 8.3% euro overvaluation and an implied fair value of 167.66–168.82. Both dossiers flag that the cached BIS series carries only 30 monthly observations, so this is a relative 30-month measure and not a long-run purchasing-power anchor.

Bilateral trade is taken directly from the injected IMF DOTS block for 2024 and not re-estimated. The mirror asymmetry (euro-area reported exports to Japan of $63.7bn versus Japan-reported imports from the euro area of $67.9bn) is normal for DOTS and does not affect the conclusion that bilateral goods trade is immaterial to the pair.

Positioning uses the CFTC reports of 21 July (the cycle snapshot retained in both dossiers for cross-currency consistency) and 28 July (the more recent print). We quote both throughout and treat the 28 July figures as operative because they postdate the intervention set-up.

Weight adjustments are documented in the Weight Adjustments table; each is within the ±0.05 limit, each carries a specific bilateral justification, and both horizons sum to exactly 1.00. Weighted scores are computed as stance score (+1 Bullish for the pair, 0 Neutral, −1 Bearish) × confidence/100 × weight, summed. Score-to-conviction mapping is inherited from both source dossiers: absolute score below 0.05 → conviction 1; 0.05–0.15 → 2; 0.15–0.30 → 3; 0.30–0.45 → 4; above 0.45 → 5.

Two web-sourced claims are load-bearing and single-sourced, and are flagged as such: (a) that the US Treasury sold euros to fund its share of the yen purchases, which appears in one secondary account and, if wrong, weakens but does not void the Factor 4 argument; and (b) the $36bn figure for the 31 July joint tranche, which one publisher reports while noting Washington's contribution remains unconfirmed. All bank and third-party forecasts cited are used for consensus benchmarking only; several retail forecast aggregators returned internally inconsistent or stale figures and were excluded from the consensus median.

Where dossier-level data are referenced (policy rates, sovereign yields, CPI, positioning, current accounts, commodity prices, catalyst dates) they are taken as given and not re-cited, per the framework's citation-integrity rule. Only sources accessed during this pair-specific research are numbered in the citation list.
